lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn un \u003cb\u003eme:
"

In a metal the bands overlap (Eg = 0): electrons always conduct. An insulator has a large Eg (diamond: 5.5 eV): at room temperature there are no electrons in the CB. A semiconductor has Eg ≈ 0.5–3 eV: some electrons move to the CB by thermal agitation, leaving holes in the VB. Choose the material.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn un sólido, los orb:
"

In a solid, the atomic orbitals of N atoms combine into N molecular orbitals so close together that they form bands. The valence band (VB) is full of electrons; the conduction band (CB) is empty. Between them there is a band gap of energy Eg. Conduction requires electrons in the CB (or holes in the VB).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa concentración de p:
"

The concentration of intrinsic carriers is ni ∝ T3/2 · exp(−Eg/2kBT). On heating a semiconductor, its conductivity increases (unlike a metal, whose conductivity falls because of greater scattering). Raise the temperature and watch more electrons promoted.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eSe \u003cb\u003edopa\:
"

Silicon is doped with impurities: phosphorus (group 15, 5 e⁻) leaves a donor level just below the CB → n-type semiconductor (carriers: electrons). Boron (group 13, 3 e⁻) creates an acceptor level above the VB → p-type (carriers: holes). With barely 1 dopant atom per 10⁷ of Si the conductivity increases enormously.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUna \u003cb\u003eunió:
"

A p–n junction forms a depletion zone with an electric field: it conducts in forward bias and blocks in reverse (diode). In an LED, CB electrons recombine with holes and emit a photon of energy ≈ Eg: λ(nm) = 1240/Eg(eV). That is why GaN (3.4 eV, ~365 nm) makes blue/white LEDs possible; GaAs (1.42 eV) emits infrared.

"
